etymology.text: From Middle High German haben, from Old High German habēn, from Proto-West Germanic *habbjan, from Proto-Germanic *habjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to grasp”). Cognates include Dutch hebben, English have, Danish have.

funFacts: German “has” hunger, thirst, fear and luck where English “is” hungry, thirsty, afraid and lucky.

Many languages have no everyday verb “to have”: Russian says у меня есть (“at me there is”), Turkish kardeşim var (“my sibling exists”), Hebrew יֵשׁ לִי (“there is to me”), Arabic عِنْدِي (“at me”). German, Greek (έχω) and English use a verb.
pitfalls: haben takes the accusative: Ich habe einen Bruder (der Bruder → einen Bruder); die, das and the plural do not change.
du hast, er hat – the b disappears in these two forms.
Age is said with sein, not haben: Ich bin 20 (Jahre alt), never *Ich habe 20 Jahre.
subtleties: Wir haben Montag / Wir haben Mai: “it is Monday / it is May” – haben for the date.
“There is/are” is es gibt, not haben (except regionally).

examples.text: Die Kinder sind hier und ihre Eltern sind dort.
examples.tr: The children are here and their parents are there.

examples.text: Max und Anna besuchen ihre Großeltern.
examples.tr: Max and Anna visit their grandparents.

etymology.text: her: from Old High German ira, from Proto-Germanic *hezōi; their: from Old High German iro.

funFacts: Her, their and polite your all sound the same in German: ihr – one reason the polite form is written with a capital.
pitfalls: ihr = her and their (and, capitalised, Ihr = your, polite). Also ihr = “you all” (pronoun) and ihr = “to her” – the context decides.
ihr Bruder = her/their brother; ihre Schwester = her/their sister.
subtleties: At the start of a sentence Ihr / Ihre can mean her, their or your (polite) – only the context helps.
profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: the possessive is the only way to say it.

address.none: the owner is not the person spoken to

profile.feeling: Ours – shared by a group I belong to.

etymology.text: From Middle High German unser, from Old High German unsēr, from Proto-West Germanic *unsar.

funFacts: unser is English our: the German keeps the n that English lost (compare uns / us).
pitfalls: The -er belongs to the stem, it is not an ending: unser Sohn, unsere Tochter, unsere Kinder.
In speech the e can drop: unsre, unsren – Wiktionary lists both.
subtleties: Vater unser (the Lord’s Prayer) keeps the old order: the possessive after the noun.
profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: the possessive is the only way to say it.

profile.feeling: Your – to several people you say ihr to.

senses.def: your (to several people you say ihr to)

etymology.text: From Middle High German iuwer, from Old High German iuwar. Compare English your, Dutch jouw, uw.

funFacts: euer is related to English your (Old English ēower).
pitfalls: With an ending the e before r usually drops: euer Sohn, but eure Tochter, euren Sohn (euere is possible but rare).
subtleties: euer goes with ihr (you all); to people you say Sie to, use Ihr.
profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: the possessive is the only way to say it.

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: Your – polite, to one or more people you say Sie to.

senses.def: your (polite, to one person you say Sie to)

examples.text: Meine Damen und Herren, Ihre Pässe bitte!
examples.tr: Ladies and gentlemen, your passports please!

examples.text: Meine Damen und Herren, Ihre Plätze sind in Reihe drei.
examples.tr: Ladies and gentlemen, your seats are in row three.

etymology.text: Capitalised ihr (“their”; from Old High German iro): the polite form uses the third person plural, like Sie (“you”) = sie (“they”).

funFacts: German politeness speaks to you as “they”: Sie haben (you have) = sie haben (they have), Ihr Haus = ihr Haus (their house).
pitfalls: Always with a capital I: Ihr Vater (your father) – ihr Vater (her/their father).
subtleties: One form for one or many people: Ihr Sohn can be said to one parent or to both.
profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: the possessive is the only way to say it.
